title: The 60-Minute Mental Marathon: What Teachers Have to Juggle
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Joel Kenyon catalogues, in granular detail, the sprawling list of non-teaching demands stacked onto a single 60-minute lesson over his nine years in the classroom, sorting them into 'justifiable,' 'semi-justifiable,' and 'non-justifiable' categories -- from legally required registers and SEND passport checks to colour-coded marking pens and mandatory hinge-point questions timed by a touring SLT member. His central move is to apply cognitive load theory, usually reserved for students, to the teacher: if working memory is a finite resource that must be protected for learning to occur, then a teacher juggling thirty students' needs while tracking a checklist of top-down initiatives is operating under the same biological constraints, and every 'small' administrative task is a cognitive intruder competing with real pedagogical judgment. He argues that many of these initiatives trace back to an 'Ofsted Mirage' -- leaders implementing practices based on hearsay about what inspectors supposedly want rather than evidence of what helps students -- and that the bitter irony is 'teach your bloody lesson, and teach it well' is rarely stated as the primary directive. Kenyon's practical ask of school leadership is 'time-neutrality': no new initiative should be added without leaders first asking what will be removed from an already overflowing bucket. The piece functions as both a wry insider account and an argument for protecting instructional attention as a scarce cognitive resource.
points: Applies cognitive load theory reflexively to teachers, not just students: a teacher's working memory is governed by the same limits, so administrative 'non-negotiables' directly compete with capacity for complex pedagogical decision-making.

Names the 'Ofsted Mirage' as a root cause -- leaders adopting practices (five pen colours, personalised feedback stamps) based on secondhand claims about what inspectors want rather than evidence of impact on learning.
Proposes 'time-neutrality' as the operating principle for new initiatives: leadership must ask what gets removed whenever something is added, rather than treating each addition as costless.
Illustrates the point with a taxonomy of real demands sorted by justifiability, showing how individually reasonable requests compound into an unmanageable checklist once stacked into one hour.
Argues that performative compliance work (proving you are teaching) increasingly displaces the actual invisible, complicated work of teaching itself.
quotes: [1] "My aim isn't just to vent, but to highlight the staggering number of tasks a teacher has to juggle in 60 minutes. I'll also be commenting on how some of these 'best practices' can actually get in the way of real learning.

[2] "This 'Ofsted Mirage' drives leaders to implement pointless tasks based on what they think inspectors want to see, rather than what the students actually need. I have always viewed the claim that 'Ofsted loves this' as a convenient fiction used to bypass any basic critical thinking.

[3] "In years of checklists, feedback loops, and data-entry requirements, the phrase 'teach your bloody lesson, and teach it well' was never once the primary directive. It is a bitter irony that in some schools, the act of teaching often falls to the bottom of the priority list.

[4] "If we accept that a student's working memory is a finite resource that must be protected to facilitate learning, we must acknowledge that a teacher's brain is governed by the same biological laws. We are effectively asking teachers to manage the cognitive load of thirty different individuals while our own is being systematically overloaded by a checklist of performative distractions.

[5] "Individually, these take a minute. Collectively, they shatter the teacher's cognitive flow and the students' focus. Every second spent navigating a spreadsheet or checking a pen is a second stolen from checking for misconceptions, providing high-quality verbal feedback, or simply connecting with a struggling learner.

[6] "When a new initiative is introduced, it should never be treated as 'one small thing.' It must be viewed as an addition to an already overflowing bucket. Leadership must begin to ask: If we add this, what are we removing?

[7] "What teachers need is not more admin or micromanaging of what takes place in their classroom. Instead, they need a repertoire of dos and don'ts that they have the autonomy to choose from during a lesson.
